q: Windward–leeward course, all marks to port, a 29er national championship in 18 knots. In the crush at the windward mark you end up passing it on the wrong side, leaving it to starboard; five lengths down the run you realise. What must you do?
a: Sail back and unwind: return upwind past the mark on the side you came, round it leaving it to port, then carry on — you may correct the error until you finish
o: Take a Two-Turns Penalty as soon as you are clear of other boats and carry on down the run — a mark error is a Part 2 breach
Retire — once you have left the zone a rounding on the wrong side can no longer be corrected
Carry on; the race committee only scores a boat NSC if she misses a mark altogether, not if she rounds it the wrong way
why: Rule 28.2: a boat may correct any error in sailing the course until she finishes; penalty turns do not replace the unwinding.
ref: RRS 28.2, RRS definition Sail the Course

fig.note: You rounded leaving the mark to starboard

q: The sailing instructions give course Start – 1 – 2 – 3 – Finish, marks to port. On the leg from mark 1 to mark 2 you pass mark 4, a mark of another course, leaving it on your starboard side. Your crew is worried. Have you broken a rule?
a: No — a mark that does not begin, bound or end the leg you are sailing may be left on either side
o: Yes — every mark laid by the race committee for the regatta must be left to port
Yes — you must go back and leave mark 4 to port before continuing to mark 2
Only if the leader left it to port; the first boat sets the required side for the fleet
why: Rule 28.1: a boat may leave on either side a mark that does not begin, bound or end the leg she is sailing.

fig.note: Leg from mark 1 to mark 2

q: In a dying breeze on a lake you misjudge the leeward gate: you sail past the outside of the right-hand gate mark without passing between the two marks, then harden up for the beat. Your crew says it does not matter which gate mark you round. Are they right?
a: No — your string must pass between the gate marks from the direction of the previous mark; you must go back and sail through the gate
o: Yes — at a gate you only have to leave one of the two marks on the required side, and you did
No — you broke rule 28 and must take a Two-Turns Penalty before continuing up the beat
No — a gate error cannot be corrected and the race committee will score you NSC
why: Definition Sail the Course: the string passes between the gate marks from the direction of the previous mark; rule 28.2 lets her correct it.
ref: RRS 28, RRS definition Sail the Course

fig.note: The left-hand gate mark is 60 m to the left, off the picture

q: A lake regatta uses a small island as a mark: the sailing instructions say "the island to starboard". The breeze is better on the island's western shore, so you sail down that side with the island on your left and carry on to the next mark. What is your position?
a: You have not sailed the course — the island had to be on your starboard side; go back and pass it correctly before you finish, or you will be scored NSC
o: You are fine — a natural feature used as a mark may be passed on either side if the SI do not name a rounding direction
You broke rule 31 by passing on the wrong side; a One-Turn Penalty puts it right
You are fine as long as you did not touch the island or its shoal water
why: Rule 28.1 and definition Sail the Course: each mark of the leg must be left on the required side; the island is a mark of the course.

fig.note: SI: the island to starboard

q: Thirty seconds after crossing the finishing line in a Melges 24 you realise that at the last gate you sailed outside the right-hand gate mark instead of between the two marks. You are still a few lengths past the line. What can you do?
a: Go back, pass through the gate correctly and cross the finishing line again — you may correct the error because you had not yet finished
o: Nothing — once you cross the finishing line your finish stands, and the race committee will score you NSC
Return to the course side of the line, take a Two-Turns Penalty and cross the line again
Nothing is needed — the gate marks do not bound the final leg to the finish
why: Rule 28.2 allows correction until she finishes; by sailing back to correct, a boat that crossed the line "continues to sail the course" and has not finished.

fig.note: You passed outside the right-hand gate mark

q: In race 3 of a J/70 regatta Blue, sail number 4471, leaves mark 2 to starboard although the marks are to be left to port, never goes back, and finishes third. Nobody protests her. What happens to her score?
a: The race committee scores her NSC without a hearing, because she did not sail the course
o: Nothing — a boat can only lose her place if another boat protests her within the time limit
She keeps third place unless the race committee protests her and a hearing finds she broke rule 28
She is scored DNF — a boat that misses a mark is treated as not having finished
why: Rule 28 and Appendix A5.1 (2025): a boat the race committee determines did not sail the course is scored NSC without a hearing.

lines: Marks were to be left to port
She never went back to correct it

q: Two minutes before your start in a Dragon fleet you sail round the committee boat, go out onto the course side of the line and come back through the line to the pre-start side to set up. The helm of the boat next to you says you now have to "unwind" around the committee boat. Does he have a point?
a: No — the string that must pass the marks correctly starts only when you begin approaching the line from the pre-start side to start; earlier manoeuvres do not count
o: Yes — every pass of a starting mark from the preparatory signal onward is part of the string and must be unwound
Yes — having been on the course side you must now return around an end of the line before you may start
Only if flag I was displayed; under flag P the string starts at the starting signal
why: Definition Sail the Course: the string runs from when she begins approaching the starting line from its pre-start side to start until she finishes.

fig.note: Two minutes before the start

q: You are close-hauled on starboard, two lengths from the windward mark, to be left to port. Red, overlapped to windward, bears away onto you; to avoid contact you bear away hard and pass the mark on the wrong side. You hail "Protest". Do you still have to go back?
a: Yes — being forced the wrong side does not relieve you of sailing the course; unwind and round the mark correctly, and protest Red for breaking rule 11
o: No — you are exonerated under rule 43.1(a) because Red compelled you to pass the mark on the wrong side
No — Red's breach means the protest committee will give you redress for the places you lost
No — but you must take a One-Turn Penalty for passing a mark of the leg on the wrong side
why: Rule 28 still applies: a boat forced past a mark on the wrong side must correct it (28.2); the other boat is penalised under rule 11.

fig.note: Red bears away onto you at the mark

q: The course board shows W2 — two laps of a windward–leeward course. You round the leeward gate after the first lap, cross the finishing line, hear no sound signal, stop and drop the jib. A friend on the committee boat shouts that you have one more lap to sail. Where do you stand?
a: You have not sailed the course; if you go on and sail the second lap your earlier crossing does not count and you finish when you cross the line after it
o: You have finished — the race committee must record the time of your first crossing of the line
You must take a Two-Turns Penalty for crossing the finishing line before completing the course
Your race is over — crossing the finishing line early is scored NSC and cannot be corrected
why: Definition Finish: a boat that crosses the line and then continues to sail the course has not finished; rule 28.2 lets her complete the course.

lines: You rounded the leeward gate once
No sound signal from the RC

q: River race, two knots of current setting across the course. Approaching the leeward mark, to be left to port, the stream sweeps you past it on the wrong side before you can round. You turn back, sail up past the mark on the same side you came down, then round it correctly leaving it to port. What else do you owe?
a: Nothing — you corrected the error before finishing, as rule 28.2 allows, and no penalty is due for the error itself
o: A One-Turn Penalty, taken as soon as you are well clear of other boats
A Two-Turns Penalty, because passing a mark on the wrong side is treated like a Part 2 breach
You must retire — a boat set onto the wrong side of a mark by current cannot correct her course
why: Rule 28.2: an error in sailing the course may be corrected before finishing; rule 44 penalties are for Part 2 and rule 31 breaches only.

q: At a Bodrum regatta the course board on the committee boat shows course 3, but you read it as course 2. You sail course 2 faultlessly — every mark of it on the correct side — and cross the finishing line fifth. What will the results show?
a: NSC — you did not sail the course that was signalled, however well you sailed the other one
o: DNF — a boat that sails the wrong course is treated as not having finished
Fifth place, unless the race committee protests you and a hearing finds you broke rule 28
DSQ after a hearing — a wrong course is always a disqualification
why: Rule 28 requires the course signalled to be sailed; Appendix A5.1 lets the race committee score NSC without a hearing.

lines: Every mark of course 2 left correctly

q: In the pile-up at the pin end of a Laser start you are squeezed out and pass outside the pin mark, leaving it to starboard; you never crossed the line between the pin and the committee boat. The fleet sails off. What is your position?
a: You have not started — go back to the pre-start side and cross the line between the pin and the committee boat before sailing on
o: You started — part of your hull crossed the extension of the line after the starting signal
You broke rule 31 by passing a starting mark on the wrong side; take a One-Turn Penalty
Sail on; the race committee will score you OCS and nothing you do now can change that
why: Definition Start and rule 28.1: a boat starts by crossing the starting line between its marks; until then she has not sailed the course.

fig.note: You passed outside the pin

q: Grey rounded the windward mark the wrong way and is now sailing back on starboard tack to unwind her rounding. You are approaching the mark close-hauled on port and will meet her. Who keeps clear?
a: You do — Grey is racing and on starboard; a boat correcting an error in sailing the course keeps her normal rights under Part 2
o: Grey — a boat sailing back to correct a course error must keep clear of boats sailing the course properly, like a boat returning to start
Grey — she is not racing while she unwinds, so she must not interfere with you
Nobody has to keep clear until Grey hails that she is unwinding; then you must give her room
why: Rule 10 applies as usual; rule 21 lists boats returning to start, taking a penalty or moving astern, not a boat correcting a rule 28 error.

q: The sailing instructions list an offset mark 1a, to be left to port, 50 m from the windward mark. In 25 knots your spinnaker hoist goes wrong and you pass 1a leaving it to starboard. Your crew says an offset mark is only an aid and does not count. Who is right?
a: You must go back — 1a begins the run and has a required side; the string must pass it to port
o: Your crew — only marks with a number in the course sequence have a required side
Your crew — an offset mark counts only for boats that have hoisted a spinnaker before reaching it
Neither — passing 1a on the wrong side is a rule 31 breach cured by a One-Turn Penalty
why: Rule 28.1: a mark that begins, bounds or ends the leg being sailed must be left on the required side; the offset mark begins the run.
ref: RRS 28.1, RRS definition Sail the Course

fig.note: Mark 1 is just above the picture; you left 1a to starboard

q: The sailing instructions define the finishing line as between the committee boat and a yellow pin buoy. A press RIB has anchored 30 m from the committee boat. You cross the line between the committee boat and the pin, passing the RIB on your right. Blue says the RIB was a mark and you left it on the wrong side. Is Blue right?
a: No — the RIB is not a mark; only objects the sailing instructions require you to leave on a specified side are marks
o: Yes — any vessel anchored by the organising authority near a line is part of that line
Yes — a race committee or press vessel is a mark whenever it displays a flag
Only if the RIB was closer to the pin than to the committee boat
why: Definition Mark: an object the sailing instructions require a boat to leave on a specified side, or an RC vessel from which a line extends.

fig.note: The SI mention only the committee boat and the pin

q: Windward–leeward course with an offset mark 1a used on the run. On the second beat you want to tack right where 1a lies, leaving it on whichever side suits the shift. May you?
a: Yes — on the beat 1a does not begin, bound or end the leg you are sailing, so it may be left on either side
o: No — once a mark is part of the course it must be left to port on every leg
No — you may pass 1a on either side only if you keep more than two hull lengths from it
Yes, but only after the leading boat has shown which side the fleet will take
why: Rule 28.1: a mark that does not begin, bound or end the leg a boat is sailing may be left on either side.

fig.note: Second beat; 1a is used only on the run

q: Marks to port. You left the windward mark to starboard and are ten lengths down the run before you notice. Your tactician proposes simply circling the mark once in the direction you first passed it. Which route actually unwinds the error?
a: Sail back upwind past the mark on the side you came down, then round it leaving it to port — the string pulled taut must lie on the port side of the mark
o: Circle the mark once in the same direction you first passed it; a full loop in either direction straightens the string
Cross to the correct side below the mark and carry on — the string only has to end up on the correct side
Return to the zone, take a One-Turn Penalty at the mark and continue down the run
why: Definition Sail the Course: the string drawn taut must pass each mark on the required side; unwinding means retracing and rounding correctly.
ref: RRS 28.2, RRS definition Sail the Course

fig.note: Marks to port; you left this mark to starboard

q: At the leeward gate of a windward–leeward course the leader passes between the gate marks and rounds the left-hand mark. You pass between the gate marks and round the right-hand one, as the breeze is better on that side. Is your rounding valid?
a: Yes — having passed between the gate marks from the direction of the previous mark you may round either of them
o: No — all boats must round the same gate mark as the leading boat
No — with marks to port only the left-hand gate mark may be rounded
Yes, but you must first hail the boats behind you which mark you are taking
why: Definition Sail the Course: pass between the gate marks from the direction of the previous mark; either mark may then be rounded.
ref: RRS 28, RRS definition Sail the Course

q: Two laps of a windward–leeward course; the finishing line lies between the committee boat and a pin halfway up the beat. On the first beat you sail straight across the finishing line on your way to the windward mark. Any consequence?
a: None — you are continuing to sail the course, so you have not finished, and the finishing marks have no required side on the first beat
o: You have finished and will be scored by that crossing unless you re-cross the line in the other direction
You must take a One-Turn Penalty for passing between finishing marks before completing the course
You must leave both finishing marks to port, since all marks of the course are to port
why: Definition Finish (c): a boat that crosses the finishing line and continues to sail the course has not finished; rule 28.1 on marks of the leg.

q: The results sheet scores you NSC in race 2: the race committee says you missed mark 3. Your GPS track shows you rounded it correctly. There are forty minutes left in the protest time limit. What is the right step?
a: Request redress within the time limit — an incorrect NSC score is an improper action of the race committee — and bring the track as evidence
o: Protest the race committee under rule 28; the protest committee will then hear it like a protest between boats
Appeal straight to the national authority, since scoring decisions are not heard by the protest committee
Nothing can be done — a score given by the race committee without a hearing is final
why: Rule 61.4(b)(1): a boat whose score was made significantly worse by an improper action or omission of the race committee may request redress.

lines: You are scored NSC in race 2
Your GPS track shows you rounded it

q: The course board on the committee boat shows 2. The sailing instructions define course 2 as Start – 1 – 2 – 3 – 1 – Finish, all marks to port. After rounding mark 3 the leader heads straight for the finishing line. Where should you go?
a: Back to mark 1 — course 2 requires mark 1 to be rounded again before the finish; the leader is making an error
o: Follow the leader to the finish — the first boat's course becomes the course for the fleet
To the finish — once every mark has been rounded at least once the course is sailed
Wait near mark 3 for the race committee to signal whether mark 1 is required again
why: Rule 28.1: a boat shall sail the course described in the sailing instructions; other boats' errors change nothing.

q: The sailing instructions say the windward mark is an orange inflatable. At the top of the beat you find an orange inflatable and, 100 m away, a yellow one. The leader rounds the yellow one and the next three boats follow. Which should you round?
a: The orange one — the mark is the object the sailing instructions describe; following the leader is no defence against NSC
o: The yellow one — once the leading boats have rounded a buoy it becomes the mark for the fleet
Either — when two buoys are in the area the race committee must accept both
The yellow one, then the orange one, to be safe
why: Rule 28.1 and definition Mark: the course is the one the sailing instructions describe, however many boats round the wrong object.

fig.title: At the windward mark
lines: SI: mark 1 is an orange inflatable
You find an orange and a yellow one
The leader rounds the yellow one

q: Two minutes before the start of a Wednesday evening club race you are luffing head to wind by the committee boat and your boom swings against its hull. Nothing is damaged. What must you do?
a: Take a One-Turn Penalty — you are racing from the preparatory signal, and a starting mark must not be touched before you start
o: Nothing — touching a mark before the starting signal is not a breach, because the race has not begun
Take a Two-Turns Penalty — contact with the committee boat is treated like a collision with another boat
Return to the pre-start side round an end of the line and start again
why: Rule 31: while racing, a boat shall not touch a starting mark before starting; racing begins at the preparatory signal; penalty under rule 44.2.

fig.note: Two minutes to the start; your boom touches the committee boat

q: Starting at the committee boat end in a 36-ft cruiser-racer, you cut it fine and your keel snags the committee boat's anchor line, which is slanting away from its bow. The hull never touches the boat. Have you broken rule 31?
a: No — the anchor line of a committee boat is not part of the mark, so touching it is not touching the mark
o: Yes — anything attached to the committee boat is part of the mark; take a One-Turn Penalty
Yes — and because you fouled her ground tackle the penalty is two turns
No, but you must retire if the anchor line stopped your boat for more than a few seconds
why: Definition Mark: an anchor line of a race committee vessel is not part of the mark; rule 31 is not broken.

fig.note: The dashed line is the committee boat's anchor line

q: You cross the finishing line in a 470, bear away to clear it and your transom bumps the pin-end finishing mark. You have not yet cleared the line. What is the right response?
a: Take a One-Turn Penalty and finish again: sail completely back to the course side, do the turn, then cross the line — you are still racing until you clear the line and marks
o: Nothing — you had already finished, and rule 31 does not apply after the finish
Take a One-Turn Penalty where you are; your finish stands because you crossed the line before the touch
Retire — a mark touched after finishing cannot be penalised by turns
why: Rule 31 covers a finishing mark after finishing while still racing; definition Finish (a): a boat taking a 44.2 penalty after crossing has not finished.

q: Rounding the windward mark in a J/24, your hull clears it by half a metre but the lazy spinnaker sheet hanging from the pole drags over the top of the buoy. Your bowman says only the hull counts. Is he right?
a: No — a boat touches a mark with any part of her hull, crew or equipment; take a One-Turn Penalty
o: Yes — since 2021 only the hull counts for touching a mark, just as for finishing
Yes — running rigging is not part of the boat for rule 31
No — and because a sail control touched the mark the penalty is two turns
why: Rule 31 is broken when any part of the boat, her equipment or crew touches the mark; the hull-only wording belongs to the definitions Start and Finish.

fig.note: Your spinnaker sheet drags over the mark

q: At a crowded leeward mark you are the outside boat, fail to give Blue the mark-room she is entitled to, touch her gunwale and, in the same tangle, bump the mark. No damage. How many turns do you owe?
a: Two turns in all — one Two-Turns Penalty covers the Part 2 breach, and for breaking rule 31 in the same incident you need not take the One-Turn Penalty as well
o: Three turns — a Two-Turns Penalty for the Part 2 breach plus a One-Turn Penalty for the mark
One turn — when a boat touches a mark the One-Turn Penalty replaces any other penalty
Four turns — a Two-Turns Penalty for each rule broken
why: Rule 44.1(a): a boat that may have broken a Part 2 rule and rule 31 in the same incident need not take the penalty for rule 31.

q: You are the inside boat at the leeward mark, overlapped since well before the zone. Red, outside, does not give you mark-room, squeezes you and your hull is pushed against the mark. Who takes a penalty?
a: Red takes a Two-Turns Penalty for breaking rule 18.2; you are exonerated for touching the mark because Red compelled you to
o: Both — Red for rule 18.2 and you a One-Turn Penalty for rule 31; the mark touch is always your own
Only you — the boat that touches the mark is the one that broke a rule
Nobody — contact caused by crowding at a mark is exonerated for all boats
why: Rule 43.1(a): a boat compelled to break a rule by another boat's breach is exonerated; the outside boat broke rule 18.2(a).

q: You touch the leeward mark with the hull in a pack of twelve boats. You carry on for about thirty seconds to get out of the traffic, then make one turn — a tack followed by a gybe — and rejoin. Was the penalty taken correctly?
a: Yes — after getting well clear of other boats as soon as possible you promptly made one turn including a tack and a gybe
o: No — the turn must be made immediately at the mark, among the other boats if need be
No — a turn for touching a mark must include two tacks, not a tack and a gybe
No — the penalty must be completed before you leave the zone of the mark you touched
why: Rule 44.2: get well clear of other boats as soon after the incident as possible, then promptly make the turn, each turn with one tack and one gybe.

q: Windward–leeward course with the starting line below the leeward gate. On the first beat, tacking in a lull, you brush one of the gate marks with your bow. Must you take a penalty?
a: No — on the first beat the gate marks do not begin, bound or end the leg you are sailing, so touching one is not a breach
o: Yes — a One-Turn Penalty; any mark of the course touched while racing breaks rule 31
Yes — a Two-Turns Penalty, because the gate is a rounding mark of the course
No — but you must sail back and pass through the gate before continuing up the beat

q: Ten seconds after starting at the committee boat end of a Star fleet, a gust heels you and your quarter touches the committee boat's topsides. You had already crossed the line. Is this a breach of rule 31?
a: Yes — the committee boat is a mark that begins the first leg; take a One-Turn Penalty after getting well clear
o: No — rule 31 only protects a starting mark before the start, and you had started
No — a committee boat is never a mark once the starting signal has been made
Yes — but the penalty is to return and start again round an end of the line

q: You have finished, cleared the finishing line and are sailing back to the committee boat to hand over a declaration form. Coming alongside, your bow bumps its hull. Do you owe a penalty?
a: No — you stopped racing when you finished and cleared the line and marks, so rule 31 no longer applies
o: Yes — a One-Turn Penalty; the committee boat is a finishing mark and you touched it after finishing
Yes — and since you cannot take turns now, the race committee will score you DSQ
Only if the committee boat was also the starting-line boat

Your crew — a float is attached to the anchor line, which is not part of the mark

o: Yes — rule 44.1(a) says a boat taking a Two-Turns Penalty need not take a penalty for rule 31
Yes — a boat taking a penalty is exonerated for any mark she touches while turning

o: A Two-Turns Penalty — two full turns are required for any breach while racing

a: Yes — rule 31 has no fault element; unless another boat compelled the touch, a One-Turn Penalty is due
o: No — a touch caused by sea state rather than by your handling is not a breach
No — in a wind of 25 knots or more rule 31 is suspended for safety
Yes — a Two-Turns Penalty, because heavy-weather contact is treated as serious

q: You round the leeward mark cleanly, harden up onto the beat, and as you sheet in your transom swings and hits the mark. You are already heading up the next leg. Have you broken rule 31?

No — only contact with the bow or the hull forward of the mast counts as touching a mark
Yes — but as the touch was after the rounding the penalty is two turns

o: Yes — rule 31 applies only to the gate mark you actually round
Yes — a spinnaker pole is not part of the boat for the purposes of rule 31
No — but the penalty is two turns because you touched a mark you were not rounding

o: A One-Turn Penalty imposed by the protest committee, taken before the next race
A 20 % scoring penalty — the protest committee cannot disqualify for touching a mark
No penalty — a touch you did not feel is not a breach

Neither — a boat that crosses the line during a penalty is scored DNF

Wait until the leader finishes and then give every other boat a finishing window
Shorten the course to the last mark the leader rounded and score the boats as they passed it

o: DNF — any boat finishing after the time limit has expired is scored as not having finished
DNF — a boat must finish within 30 minutes of the winner unless the SI say otherwise

o: Yes — the finishing line extends to the windward mark when it lies within 50 m of the pin

No — the protest committee must order the race to be resailed

fig.title: After a 20° shift
lines: Flag C + green triangle at mark 2

q: Halfway up the first beat you see the mark-laying boat lift the windward mark and re-lay it 150 m to the right, with no flag C anywhere and the original mark in no way missing or adrift. Several boats on the left are now badly placed. Was that a proper race committee action?
a: No — rule 33 allows changing only the next leg, signalled before boats begin it, and rule 34 covers only a mark missing or out of position
o: Yes — the race committee may move any mark at any time to keep the beat square to the wind
Yes — rule 34 allows a mark to be relaid wherever the race committee thinks best
No — but only because the mark was moved more than 100 m; a smaller adjustment needs no signal
why: Rule 33 permits changing the next leg, signalled before boats begin it; rule 34 permits repositioning only a mark missing or out of position.

fig.title: First beat
lines: No flag C; mark was not adrift

q: The sailing instructions say course changes will be signalled under rule 33. At mark 1 a committee boat shows flag C with repeated sounds, a red rectangle and a board with 190. Mark 2 was on 230° from mark 1. Where do you look for mark 2 now?
a: On a bearing of 190° from mark 1 — the leg has been changed to port, and the board gives the new compass bearing
o: On a bearing of 230° still — the red rectangle only warns that mark 2 is to be left to port
On a bearing of 270° — the red rectangle means 40° further to starboard
At mark 1 itself — flag C with a bearing means the course is shortened to finish here
why: Rule 33(a): the change of direction is signalled by the new compass bearing and/or a red rectangle (port) or green triangle (starboard).

q: Running towards mark 2 you cannot find it; where it should be there is a committee RIB displaying flag M and making repetitive sound signals. What do you do?
a: Treat the RIB as mark 2 — leave it on the required side and continue the course
o: Sail to where mark 2 was laid according to the sailing instructions and round that position
Stop and wait: flag M means the race will be abandoned once all boats have gathered
Pass the RIB on either side; a committee vessel is never a mark unless it anchors a line
why: Rule 34(b): a missing mark may be replaced by an object displaying flag M with repetitive sound signals; it is then the mark.

fig.note: Mark 2 has disappeared; the RIB makes repeated sound signals

q: During the second lap the leeward mark drags 80 m downwind in a gust. The mark-laying boat tows it back to its original position without any flag or sound signal. Blue says the race committee had to signal the move with flag C. Is Blue right?
a: No — a mark out of position may be moved back to its correct position without a signal; flag C is for changing the next leg
o: Yes — any movement of a mark while boats are racing must be signalled with flag C
Yes — the race committee should instead have abandoned the race
No — but the mark should have been replaced by a vessel with flag M, not towed back
why: Rule 34(a): if a mark is missing or out of position the RC shall, if possible, replace it in its correct position; no signal is required.

q: The windward mark has sunk. There is no spare buoy and the only committee RIB is busy with a capsized Optimist. The leaders are approaching the spot where the mark was. What should the race committee do?
a: If it cannot put a replacement or a vessel with flag M in position, it should abandon the race under rule 32.1(c), because a mark is missing
o: Let the boats round the GPS position of the mark; the sailing instructions give its coordinates
Shorten the course with flag S at the leeward mark after the boats have come back down
Score the boats by their order of arrival at the spot and continue to the next mark
why: Rule 34: replace a missing mark or substitute an object with flag M if possible; otherwise rule 32.1(c) — abandon because a mark is missing.

fig.title: Windward mark sunk
lines: Only RIB busy with a capsized Optimist

q: Mark 3 has gone adrift. A committee RIB with flag M and repeated sound signals has anchored about 100 m from where the mark used to be. You round the empty spot where mark 3 was, ignoring the RIB, and sail on. How will you be scored?
a: NSC — the RIB with flag M replaced the mark, so you did not sail the course
o: By your finishing place — the sailing instructions give the mark's position, and you rounded it
By your finishing place, since the RIB was not in the mark's exact position
DNF — a boat that does not round the replacement vessel is treated as not finishing
why: Rule 34(b): an object displaying flag M replaces the missing mark; rule 28 and A5.1 — a boat that does not sail the course is scored NSC.

fig.note: You rounded the empty spot where mark 3 used to be

q: In race 2 you fouled Blue on port tack and took a Two-Turns Penalty. Twenty minutes later the race was abandoned and is now being resailed. Blue says you must take the two turns again at the start of the resail. Must you?
a: No — a breach in the original race is not a reason to penalise a boat in the resail, except for rules 2, 30.2, 30.4, 69 or rule 14 with serious damage or injury
o: Yes — penalties taken in an abandoned race do not count and must be repeated
Yes — but one turn is enough the second time
No — because you took the penalty at the time; had you not, you would be disqualified from the resail
why: Rule 36(b): breaches in the original race are not a reason to penalise a boat in the resail, with the listed exceptions.

fig.title: Race 2 abandoned, now resailed
lines: You fouled Blue and took two turns

q: In the original race Grey, on port, hit you at speed and holed your topsides — a clear breach of rule 14 with serious damage. The race was then abandoned for lack of wind and resailed. Grey sails the resail and says the abandonment wiped the slate clean. Is she right?
a: No — rule 36 excepts rule 14 breaches that caused serious damage or injury; Grey can still be penalised for the original incident
o: Yes — a breach in an abandoned race can never be penalised in the resail
Yes — but you can request redress in the resail for the damage
No — because any contact in an abandoned race carries over, with or without damage
why: Rule 36(b): a boat may still be penalised for a breach of rules 2, 30.2, 30.4, 69 or rule 14 when she caused serious damage or injury.

fig.title: Original race, then resail
lines: Grey on port hit you at speed

q: Under a black flag you were in the triangle in the last minute and the race committee displayed your sail number after the general recall. The class now restarts. May you sail the restart?
a: No — a boat disqualified under rule 30.4 may not sail in the restart; rule 36 makes 30.4 the one breach that bars a boat from a restarted race
o: Yes — a general recall cancels all starting penalties, including the black flag
Yes — but you must start at least one minute after the starting signal
No — and you are also excluded from the rest of the regatta
why: Rule 36(a): a breach in the original race does not prevent a boat from competing in a restart, except a breach of rule 30.4.

fig.title: Black flag start, general recall
lines: In the triangle in the last minute

q: In a race later abandoned for a wind shift, Red deliberately sailed through the finishing area to block a rival, breaking rule 2. The race is resailed. Red says the abandonment ends the matter. Does it?
a: No — rule 36 keeps rule 2 breaches alive: Red can still be penalised for the original race despite the abandonment
o: Yes — once a race is abandoned nothing that happened in it can be penalised
Yes — unless the rival requests redress in the resail
No — but only a report under rule 69 can now be made, not a protest
why: Rule 36(b): a breach of rule 2, 30.2, 30.4, 69 or rule 14 with serious damage in the original race may still be penalised after a resail.

q: Your hull has crossed the finishing line and you are turning away on port tack, still within a length of the pin. Blue, finishing on starboard, is converging. Who keeps clear?
a: You do — until you clear the finishing line and marks you are still racing, so rule 10 applies as usual between you
o: Blue — a boat that has finished has right of way over boats still finishing
Nobody — once a boat's hull has crossed the line the rules of Part 2 no longer apply to her
Blue — she must not interfere with a boat that has finished, under rule 23.1
why: Definition Racing: a boat is racing until she finishes and clears the line and marks; Part 2 applies, rule 10 (opposite tacks).

fig.note: You have crossed but not yet cleared the line

q: The sailing instructions for a coastal race say: "Mark 1 to port, mark 2 to starboard, mark 3 to port." Your crew assumes all marks are to port and plans to round mark 2 turning left. What is correct?
a: Round mark 2 leaving it to starboard, turning right — each mark must be left on the side the sailing instructions specify for it
o: Round all marks to port — marks of a course are always left on the same side
Round mark 2 either side — a single mark with a different side does not bound a leg
Round mark 2 to port and take a One-Turn Penalty for the error
why: Rule 28.1 and definition Sail the Course: each mark is passed on its required side as given in the sailing instructions.

fig.title: SI 10.2: the course
lines: Crew plans to turn left at mark 2

q: The sailing instructions name mark 2 as a rounding mark; the course doubles back from it towards mark 1. In a foul tide you turn back 50 m short of mark 2, well on its correct side, and head for mark 1. Have you sailed the leg?
a: No — the string must touch each rounding mark; by turning short of mark 2 you never passed it, and you must go back and round it before you finish
o: Yes — the string stays on the correct side of mark 2, so the leg is sailed
Yes — a rounding mark need only be approached within hailing distance
No — and because you turned short of a mark you are scored DNF
why: Definition Sail the Course: the string touches each mark the SI designate a rounding mark; rule 28.2 allows the error to be corrected.
ref: RRS 28, RRS definition Sail the Course

fig.note: You turned back 50 m short of mark 2

q: At mark 2 the committee boat shows flag C with repeated sounds, a board with 040 and a minus sign. The leg to mark 3 was 1.2 miles on 020°. What do you now know about the leg to mark 3?
a: It now lies on 040° and is shorter than 1.2 miles — mark 3 has been moved to starboard and closer
o: It lies on 040° and is 1.2 miles minus 40 metres long
It lies 40° to port of the old bearing and is shorter
It is unchanged — the signal concerns the leg after mark 3
why: Rule 33(a) and (b): flag C with a new compass bearing changes the direction, and "−" means the leg has been shortened.

fig.title: At mark 2
lines: Old leg to mark 3: 1.2 M on 020°

q: You pass between the leeward gate marks and gybe round the right-hand mark, leaving it to starboard. Your crew protests that the sailing instructions say "marks to port". Did you round correctly?
a: Yes — at a gate a boat passes between the marks and may round either; rounding the right-hand mark means leaving it to starboard, which the gate definition allows
o: No — with marks to port the right-hand gate mark may only be passed on your port side
No — you should have gone round the outside of the right-hand mark to keep it to port
Yes, but only because your crew had not hailed which mark to take
why: Definition Sail the Course: at a gate the string passes between the marks from the previous mark and then round either gate mark.
ref: RRS 28, RRS definition Sail the Course

fig.note: The left-hand gate mark is off the picture to the left

q: In a Hobie 16 race the only boat to cross the finishing line within the 90-minute time limit is later scored NSC because she left mark 3 on the wrong side. Three other boats crossed the line a few minutes after the time limit. Is the race valid?
a: No — a race is scored only if a boat started, sailed the course and finished within the time limit; an NSC boat did not sail the course, so the race must be abandoned
o: Yes — she crossed the finishing line within the time limit, and that is what the time limit measures
Yes — the first of the three later boats is treated as having finished within the limit
No — but the race committee may score the three boats by their order of crossing
why: Rule 35 and 90.3(a): the race stands only if one boat starts, sails the course and finishes within the time limit; otherwise it is abandoned.

fig.title: Time limit 90 min
lines: Only one boat crossed within 90 min
She is scored NSC (mark 3 wrong side)
Three boats crossed a few minutes later

q: A change of course was correctly signalled with flag C at the windward mark before you got there, but you did not notice it. You sailed to the original leeward mark, which had been removed, found nothing and eventually finished. How will you be scored?
a: NSC — the changed course is the course; a boat that does not see a correctly made signal is still bound by it
o: By your finishing place — a boat that could not see the new mark is not responsible for the change
Average points — missing a signal is a ground for redress
DNF — you did not finish the course as originally described
why: Rule 33 changes the course when signalled before boats begin the leg; rule 28 requires that course to be sailed; A5.1 — NSC.

fig.title: Flag C at the windward mark
lines: Sailed to the old leeward mark: removed

q: You capsize while tacking at the windward mark and, still capsized, drift past the mark on the wrong side; you right the boat three lengths beyond it. Your crew says a capsized boat is not sailing, so the drift does not count. Who is right?
a: You must unwind — the string of your track passed the mark on the wrong side, however you got there; sail back and round it correctly
o: Your crew — a boat is not sailing the course while capsized, so her drift is ignored
Your crew — but you must take a One-Turn Penalty for passing the mark on the wrong side
Nobody can say — ask the race committee for a ruling before continuing
why: Definition Sail the Course: the string represents the boat's track from the start to the finish; rule 28.2 lets her correct the error before finishing.
ref: RRS 28.2, RRS definition Sail the Course

fig.note: You capsized at the mark and drifted past it on the wrong side

q: The race committee signals a general recall with the First Substitute and two sounds. Sailing back, you bump the committee boat while jostling at its stern. Must you take a One-Turn Penalty?
a: No — the general recall ended your racing, so rule 31 no longer applied when you touched the committee boat
o: Yes — you remain racing until the First Substitute is lowered and the new warning signal is made
Yes — the committee boat is a starting mark from the first preparatory signal until the class finally starts
No — but you must return around an end of the line before the new start
why: Definition Racing: a boat stops racing when a general recall is signalled; rule 31 applies only while racing.
